lead: A transaction is a signed instruction to move coins. It starts in a wallet, spreads by gossip to many nodes, waits in a pool of unconfirmed transactions, and enters a block only when a miner picks it. The miner is paid to choose and to order, and the network accepts the block only after every other node rechecks it. This life cycle explains why a crypto payment is quick to send but slow to become final, and why the fee you offer decides how long you wait. Exchange deposit credits and refund waits both follow this flow.
prereq: You need: what a block holds (Unit 1), hashing and digital signatures (Unit 2), and how nodes find each other and gossip, from 3.1.

sections.h3: A transaction is built, signed, then gossiped

blocks.text: A wallet does not hold coins. It holds keys and points to coins on the chain called unspent transaction outputs, or UTXOs. A UTXO is an amount locked to an address that no transaction has spent yet. To pay someone, the wallet builds a transaction with three parts: inputs (the UTXOs being spent), outputs (amount plus receiver address), and a fee. The inputs must add up to at least the outputs plus the fee.

The wallet then signs. It hashes the transaction data and signs that hash with the sender's private key. Any node can verify the signature with the sender's public key. The signature covers the amounts and the recipient, so changing even one satoshi breaks it.

items: Check the signature against the public keys of the inputs.
Check the spending conditions on each input are satisfied.
Check each input exists on the chain and is still unspent.
Check inputs ≥ outputs, so the fee is not negative.
Check the same input is not already waiting in the mempool (double spend).

blocks.text: A transaction that passes all checks goes into the node's mempool, the pool of valid but unconfirmed transactions, and is passed to other peers. A transaction that fails is dropped; nobody sends a rejection message. Mempools are local, so two nodes may hold different sets at the same moment. That is normal and not a disagreement about history.

sections.h3: The fee is size times rate

blocks.text: fee = size (bytes) × fee rate (satoshi per byte)
blocks.where: fee is the total satoshi given to the miner; size is the transaction's size in bytes; fee rate is the price the sender offers for one byte of block space. 1 bitcoin = 100,000,000 satoshi.

blocks.text: A block has a size limit, so the scarce thing miners sell is space, not transactions. That is why the price is quoted per byte. A transaction with twice the size at the same rate pays twice the fee.

items: Miners rank by fee rate, not by total fee. A small transaction at 30 sat/byte beats a large one at 10 sat/byte.
When the mempool is crowded, senders bid the rate up; when it is empty, even the minimum rate gets in.
Fee is not deducted as a separate output. It is the gap between inputs and outputs, and the miner claims it.
Place the coinbase transaction first. It creates the block reward plus the fees of all included transactions.
Fill the rest of the block from the mempool, highest fee rate first, until the size limit is reached.
Write the previous block hash, the Merkle root of the transactions, a timestamp, the target and a nonce.
Change the nonce until the block hash falls below the target. This is the Proof of Work of 3.4.
Broadcast the finished block to peers.

blocks.text: Every other node now validates the whole block, not just the puzzle: correct proof of work, every transaction valid, no double spend inside the block or against the chain, correct coinbase amount. A valid block is added to the chain tip. An invalid one is rejected and the miner's whole reward is lost, which is why serious miners also run a full node.

Confirmations are counted in blocks. The block that holds your transaction gives one confirmation; each block mined on top adds one more. Six is a common convention for large amounts, not a rule of the protocol.

The coinbase output has maturity: in Bitcoin it can be spent only after 100 more blocks. Two miners may also find blocks at the same height. Nodes follow one, and the other becomes a stale or orphan block: its coinbase is worthless and its transactions go back to the mempool.

items: Ordering: the miner decides which transactions go in and in what sequence.
Extension: the miner adds the next block and so lengthens the heaviest chain.
Issuance: the coinbase transaction creates new coins at a fixed schedule.
Collection: the miner takes the fee gap of every transaction it includes.

blocks.text: A full node that does not mine validates every transaction and block and keeps the rules. A miner that does not validate is blind: it can be handed an invalid chain and waste its hash power building on top of it. Miners supply ordering; full nodes supply the checking that makes the ordering trustworthy.
One flaw belongs here. A third party can alter a signature without invalidating the transaction, which changes its transaction id. This is transaction malleability, and SegWit fixes it (see Unit 4).

spec.aria: Three transaction boxes sized by bytes, T1 250, T2 500, T3 1000, with their fee rates 20, 30 and 10 satoshi per byte, then a 1750-byte block filled in the order T2, T1, T3.

examples.question: A mempool holds three transactions. T1 is 250 bytes with a fee of 5000 satoshi. T2 is 500 bytes with a fee of 15000 satoshi. T3 is 1000 bytes with a fee of 10000 satoshi. (a) Find the fee rate of each. (b) Give the order a profit-maximising miner puts them in a block. (c) Find the total size, total fee and average fee rate of that block.
steps: Fee rate = fee ÷ size, in satoshi per byte.
Rank by fee rate: T2 (30) first, then T1 (20), then T3 (10). Ordering by total fee instead would put T3 second and waste block space on 10 sat/byte.
examples.answer: Fee rates are 20, 30 and 10 sat/byte; the order is T2, T1, T3; the block is 1750 bytes carrying 30000 satoshi, about 17.14 sat/byte.
examples.check:
t1_size, t1_fee = 250, 5000
t2_size, t2_fee = 500, 15000
t3_size, t3_fee = 1000, 10000
print(t1_fee / t1_size)
print(t2_fee / t2_size)
print(t3_fee / t3_size)
total_size = t1_size + t2_size + t3_size
total_fee = t1_fee + t2_fee + t3_fee
print(total_size)
print(total_fee)
print(round(total_fee / total_size, 2))

traps: Treating the fee as a fixed amount. It is size × rate, so the same rate on a bigger transaction costs more.
Ranking by total fee instead of fee rate. The 15000 satoshi fee looks bigger, but per byte the small transaction may pay more.
Calling a transaction final after one block. Confirmations are blocks on top, and six is a convention, not a protocol rule.
Expecting a stale block to pay its miner. Its coinbase is invalid and its transactions return to the mempool.
Spending mining income at once. The coinbase output matures only after 100 further blocks in Bitcoin.

quiz.a: The pool of valid but not yet confirmed transactions held by a node, from which miners select.

quiz.q: Why is the fee specified per byte rather than per transaction?
quiz.a: Block space is the limited resource. Per-byte pricing charges a transaction for the space it actually occupies, so large transactions pay more and miners can compare competing transactions fairly.

quiz.q: Transaction A is 400 bytes with a fee of 8000 satoshi. Transaction B is 200 bytes with a fee of 6000 satoshi. Which does a miner prefer, and what is the difference in fee rate?
quiz.a: A: 8000 ÷ 400 = 20 sat/byte. B: 6000 ÷ 200 = 30 sat/byte. The miner prefers B; the difference is 10 sat/byte.

quiz.q: A block holds 1750 bytes and collects 30000 satoshi in fees. What fee rate does that represent? If a transaction of 500 bytes is added at that rate, what fee does it pay?
quiz.a: 30000 ÷ 1750 ≈ 17.14 sat/byte. At that rate a 500-byte transaction pays 500 × 17.14 ≈ 8570 satoshi.

quiz.q: How many confirmations does a transaction have once the block holding it plus five more blocks are on the chain?
quiz.a: Six confirmations: one for its own block and one for each block built on top.

quiz.q: Why does a miner need to run a full validating node even though its job is only to find blocks?
quiz.a: Without validation the miner cannot tell a valid chain tip from an invalid one. It could spend hash power extending an invalid block, and the network would reject its block, losing the whole reward. Validation also tells it which mempool transactions are spendable, so its block is not rejected for a double spend.

quiz.q: Two miners find blocks at the same height. Explain what the network does and what happens to the losing block.
quiz.a: Nodes keep the first valid block they see and may switch to the other branch if it later becomes longer. The block left off the chosen chain becomes stale: its coinbase reward is invalid and its transactions go back to the mempool for a later block.

quiz.q: Name the four jobs a miner performs.
quiz.a: Ordering transactions, extending the chain, issuing new coins through the coinbase transaction, and collecting fees.

beyond: Not for the exam. Wallets estimate the fee rate from recent blocks and from the mempool, so the number you see in an app is a live market price. Replace-by-fee lets a sender raise the rate on an unconfirmed transaction by paying more. Researchers study mempool congestion as a queueing problem and study ordering power itself, since whoever orders can sometimes profit from placing their own transactions carefully. On Ethereum this became the study of maximal extractable value and block building markets. Useful search terms: mempool fee estimation, replace-by-fee, coinbase maturity, maximal extractable value.
